text:
Jibangshu Paul vs National Investigation Agency (Gauhati High Court, 2011-07-27). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Bail cancelled by Special NIA Court due to addition of UA(P) Act sections
Summary: Bail earlier granted to Jibangshu Paul under IPC sections was cancelled after UA(P) Act sections were added. Court ruled fresh bail was needed for the added serious offences.
Facts: Jibangshu Paul was apprehended carrying Rs. 32,11,000 in cash, suspected to be intended for the DHD(J) militant group. He was earlier granted bail for IPC sections. Later, serious sections under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act were added, and NIA sought his re-arrest. The Special Court directed custody, rejecting his prayer to continue on earlier bail.
Legal issues: Whether fresh bail is needed when new, more serious penal sections are added; Whether cancellation of earlier bail is required due to lack of jurisdiction; Powers of the Special Court under NIA Act to take cognizance and grant bail
Reasoning: The court held that newly added serious UA(P) Act offences required separate consideration and the Special Judge could not continue prior bail orders granted under IPC sections. Hence, fresh bail was required, and custody was ordered.
Principles: Addition of new penal sections requires fresh bail consideration; Special Court’s power to override earlier bail in light of new charges; Bail cancellation permissible if initial court lacked jurisdiction

State By The Superintendent Of Police vs Mehboob Batcha And Others (Madras High Court, 1997-09-30). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Bail granted earlier to A3, A6, A8, and A10 was cancelled; fresh bail plea of A1 and A2 was rejected
Summary: Madras High Court cancelled the bail granted to four convicted accused in a custodial rape case and rejected bail for two others, citing gravity of offence and societal impact.
Facts: The case involves custodial rape of a woman by multiple accused including police officials. The trial court convicted several accused under IPC sections for rape and related offences. Accused were on bail during investigation and trial. After conviction, some accused got bail under suspension of sentence, which the prosecution challenged seeking cancellation.
Legal issues: Whether suspension of sentence requires detailed reasons under Section 389(1) CrPC; Whether bail granted post-conviction can be cancelled under Section 439(2) CrPC; What are the relevant considerations in cancelling bail post-conviction
Reasoning: The court held that due to the grave nature of the offence (custodial rape), impact on victim and society, and high punishment awarded, continuation of bail would not be justified. There was no reason to believe that the conviction was unsustainable at this stage, and hence bail was cancelled and further relief denied.

text:
Hyderali vs State Of Kerala (Kerala High Court, 2008-08-05). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Anticipatory bail rejected despite parity arguments due to gravity of economic fraud and need for custodial interrogation
Summary: Kerala High Court rejected anticipatory bail for a contractor accused in a massive forged bill scam, citing the need for custodial interrogation and gravity of offence despite parity claims.
Facts: Hyderali, a government contractor, was accused in a large-scale economic fraud involving forged petroleum bills used to claim government money. Fake bills allegedly prepared by the first accused were used by various officials and contractors, including Hyderali, to claim crores from the exchequer. The first accused died under suspicious circumstances after giving detailed confessions.
Legal issues: Whether anticipatory bail can be granted when similarly placed co-accused were granted bail; Whether custodial interrogation is necessary in economic offences involving documentary evidence; Whether parity in bail can override the gravity of allegations and investigative needs
Reasoning: The court ruled that despite other co-accused getting anticipatory bail, the petitioner could not be treated similarly due to the serious nature of allegations, need for custodial interrogation, and discovery of systemic sabotage of investigation. The court emphasized that custodial interrogation is a legitimate investigative tool and anticipatory bail cannot be granted solely based on parity.
Principles: Custodial interrogation is legitimate and may be essential even when co-accused have bail; Anticipatory bail cannot be granted solely based on parity; Courts may initiate judicial monitoring of investigations under Sakiri Vasu principle

Rashbehari Karmakar vs Indrajit Mukherjee And Anr. (Calcutta High Court, 2002-07-12). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Bail previously granted to police officer Indrajit Mukherjee was upheld despite petition for cancellation alleging threats and tampering
Summary: Calcutta High Court refused to cancel bail of a police officer accused in a custodial torture case, citing lack of compelling new grounds or threat to justice.
Facts: The petitioner, a government employee, alleged that he was brutally tortured and castrated in police custody by multiple officers due to his involvement in an agitation. Indrajit Mukherjee, then OC of Kalna PS, was among those charged. The petitioner sought cancellation of bail granted to Mukherjee, alleging post-release intimidation.
Legal issues: Whether bail should be cancelled under Section 439(2) CrPC due to post-release threats and misuse of liberty; Whether the grant of interim and confirmed bail without referencing prior anticipatory bail rejection was improper; What constitutes cogent and overwhelming grounds for bail cancellation
Reasoning: The court found no cogent or overwhelming reason to cancel bail, noting that the alleged threats did not directly impact trial or investigation. Despite serious allegations, absence of new evidence of misuse of liberty meant bail could not be revoked.
Principles: Difference between grant and cancellation of bail; Bail once granted cannot be cancelled lightly; cogent reasons are required; Interim bail can be confirmed after reviewing case diary

Smt. Shankri Devi Age 62 Years vs Union Territory Of J&K Through SHO (High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh at Jammu, 2023-06-12). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Review of earlier rejection of bail under Section 439 CrPC dismissed; no clerical or legal error found in earlier order rejecting bail
Summary: Jammu & Kashmir High Court rejected the review plea for bail in a murder case, affirming its prior order and holding that no legal error existed to justify reconsideration.
Facts: Shankri Devi and co-accused were charged with the murder of Sita Devi, allegedly beaten to death by Mangal Singh with support from others including the petitioner. Petitioners sought review of the High Court's earlier order rejecting bail, citing overlooked witness testimony and their gender-based entitlement under Section 437 CrPC.
Legal issues: Whether the court’s earlier bail rejection order contained errors apparent on the face of the record; Whether female accused are entitled to bail under proviso to Section 437 CrPC; Whether review of bail order under Section 362 CrPC is maintainable
Reasoning: The court held that its earlier rejection of bail was reasoned and based on witness testimonies. No clerical or apparent legal error warranted review. It emphasized that being a woman accused in a serious offence like murder does not automatically justify bail.
Principles: Bail once rejected cannot be reviewed except to correct clerical errors under Section 362 CrPC; Proviso to Section 437 CrPC does not guarantee bail to women in all serious offences; Credibility of witnesses cannot be evaluated in bail proceedings

text:
Hardeep Singh @ Dipi vs State Of Punjab (Punjab and Haryana High Court, 2021-04-29). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Juvenile accused granted bail under Section 12 of the JJ Act after nearly one year in detention; no threat to justice or risk to welfare found
Summary: Punjab & Haryana High Court granted bail to a juvenile accused in a murder case, ruling that prolonged detention violated Section 12 of the JJ Act since no continuing risk or injustice was found.
Facts: Hardeep Singh @ Dipi, a juvenile, was implicated in a gang-related robbery and murder based on co-accused confessions. He had been in a juvenile protection home for almost a year. Previous courts denied bail citing societal risk and psychological harm. The High Court reversed this, applying the JJ Act’s presumption in favour of bail for children.
Legal issues: Whether Section 12 of the Juvenile Justice Act mandates bail unless specific exceptions apply; Whether association with adult co-accused justifies continued detention of a juvenile; Whether heinousness of the offence overrides statutory bail rights under the JJ Act
Reasoning: The court emphasized that Section 12 of the JJ Act mandates bail for juveniles unless release would expose them to danger or defeat justice. The petitioner had not inflicted fatal injuries and co-accused were already in custody, so no such danger remained. Detention beyond one year was held unjustified.
Principles: Section 12 of JJ Act mandates bail to juveniles unless specific risks apply; Heinous nature of offence alone does not bar juvenile bail under JJ Act; Courts must prioritize welfare and statutory safeguards for juveniles

Bharath Kumar R @ Bande @ Bharath vs The State Of Karnataka (Karnataka High Court, 2022-07-11). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Bail rejected for accused no.1 despite co-accused having bail; court held he was the main conspirator and absconded, destroying evidence
Summary: Karnataka High Court rejected bail to the alleged mastermind in a murder-for-hire case, citing his absconding, role in the crime, and lack of cooperation with investigators.
Facts: Bharath Kumar was accused of conspiring to murder Harish by paying 'supari' to co-accused. He was absconding after his anticipatory bail was denied and surrendered only months later. He allegedly failed to cooperate with police, and the case involves joint recovery of blood-stained weapons linking accused to the crime.
Legal issues: Whether the petitioner, being the main conspirator, is entitled to bail on parity with co-accused; Whether prolonged abscondence and non-cooperation affects bail eligibility; Whether discretionary bail can be denied despite other accused getting bail
Reasoning: The court found that the accused was the main conspirator who paid for the murder, remained absconding, and failed to cooperate in investigation. Parity with co-accused was rejected since those granted bail had less direct roles. Court emphasized the gravity of conspiracy and potential threat to witnesses.
Principles: Ground of parity does not apply where accused’s role and conduct differ substantially; Discretionary relief of bail can be denied despite co-accused being released; Absconding and non-cooperation are valid grounds for denying bail

text:
V.S. Norti And Ors. vs State Of Karnataka (Karnataka High Court, 1989-02-09). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Anticipatory bail rejected for police officers accused of custodial murder; court followed Supreme Court precedent disallowing such bail when investigation is incomplete
Summary: Karnataka High Court denied anticipatory bail to police officers accused of custodial murder, citing binding precedent against such bail when investigation is ongoing.
Facts: Petitioners, police personnel, were accused of murdering a suspect named Guddappa in custody at Ranebennur Police Station. The defense argued no prima facie evidence existed for a murder charge and sought anticipatory bail, contending it should at most be a case under Section 330 IPC. The court held the investigation was still ongoing and applied the Supreme Court's ruling that anticipatory bail should not be granted in murder cases during incomplete investigation.
Legal issues: Whether anticipatory bail can be granted in a custodial murder case with ongoing investigation; Whether Section 438 CrPC empowers courts to override public interest and procedural considerations; Interpretation of Supreme Court rulings as binding precedent under Article 141
Reasoning: The court found that the case involved custodial death under investigation by a specialized unit. Following the precedent in Kiran Devi v. State of Rajasthan, the court held anticipatory bail is impermissible in murder cases during incomplete investigation and emphasized judicial discipline under Article 141 of the Constitution.
Principles: Anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC is exceptional and must not be used to interfere with ongoing murder investigations; Supreme Court's interpretation is binding under Article 141 of the Constitution; Custodial deaths require stricter scrutiny and bar on pre-arrest bail

text:
Aslam Babalal Desai vs State Of Maharashtra (Supreme Court of India, 1992-09-15). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Bail granted under Section 167(2) CrPC upheld; cancellation cannot be done merely on filing of charge-sheet
Summary: Supreme Court ruled that default bail under Section 167(2) CrPC cannot be cancelled merely upon charge-sheet filing; special grounds are required to justify such cancellation.
Facts: Aslam Babalal Desai was arrested in connection with a murder case and granted default bail under Section 167(2) CrPC due to failure by the police to file the charge-sheet within 90 days. The State later filed the charge-sheet and sought cancellation of bail under Section 439(2). The High Court cancelled the bail, which was challenged before the Supreme Court.
Legal issues: Whether default bail under Section 167(2) CrPC can be cancelled solely on filing of the charge-sheet; Whether bail under Section 167(2) is deemed to be under Chapter XXXIII and subject to cancellation under Sections 437(5) or 439(2); Whether liberty granted due to prosecutorial delay can be easily revoked
Reasoning: The Court held that bail granted under Section 167(2) cannot be cancelled merely due to the filing of the charge-sheet. Cancellation must be based on valid grounds like tampering with evidence, threat to witnesses, or likelihood of fleeing. Legislative intent was to instil urgency in investigation and protect individual liberty.
Principles: Bail under Section 167(2) CrPC is deemed to be under Chapter XXXIII; Cancellation of bail requires grounds under Section 437(5) or 439(2), not mere filing of charge-sheet; Legislative aim of Section 167 is to ensure investigation is completed within time limits and to protect liberty

text:
Anil Kumar Alias Neelu vs State Of Himachal Pradesh (Himachal Pradesh High Court, 2019-09-09). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Regular bail granted for intermediate quantity heroin case under NDPS Act after consideration of custody duration and lack of necessity for further custodial interrogation
Summary: Himachal Pradesh High Court granted bail to an accused in an NDPS case involving intermediate quantity heroin, noting lack of custodial requirement and completion of investigation.
Facts: The petitioner was arrested with 6.71 grams of heroin along with two others during a police chase. The heroin was confirmed by a forensic report. The petitioner had prior NDPS cases, but no details were provided. Bail was sought under Section 439 CrPC after charge-sheet was filed.
Legal issues: Whether judicial custody serves any purpose in NDPS cases involving intermediate quantity; Whether rigours of Section 37 NDPS Act apply to intermediate quantity; Whether prior cases without detailed status preclude bail
Reasoning: The court noted that the quantity was intermediate and not commercial, hence Section 37 did not apply. Since the petitioner had been in custody since April and charge-sheet had been filed, the court saw no purpose in continued detention and granted bail.
Principles: Section 37 NDPS Act rigour not applicable for intermediate quantity; Bail in intermediate quantity NDPS cases to be considered like other penal offences; Parity cannot be sole ground for bail; individual role and facts must be assessed

text:
Shahzad Hasan Khan vs Ishtiaq Hasan Khan & Anr (Supreme Court of India, 1987-04-28). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Supreme Court cancelled bail granted by High Court, citing breach of judicial discipline and serious allegations of evidence tampering
Summary: Supreme Court set aside High Court's bail order in a murder case, reaffirming the need for judicial consistency and consideration of tampering risks in serious offences.
Facts: Ishtiaq Hasan Khan was accused in a public daylight murder case and had multiple bail applications rejected. A High Court judge later granted bail, disregarding judicial convention to refer successive bail pleas to the same judge. The Supreme Court found that trial delays were due to accused tactics and that serious allegations of witness tampering were ignored by the High Court.
Legal issues: Whether successive bail applications should be heard by the same judge who decided earlier applications; Whether liberty alone justifies bail in serious offences despite procedural abuse; Whether allegations of tampering with witnesses preclude bail
Reasoning: The Supreme Court held that judicial discipline required the successive bail application to be placed before the same judge. It found the High Court erred by ignoring prior rejections, disregarding tampering allegations, and being swayed solely by the notion of liberty. The bail order was set aside and custody was ordered.
Principles: Successive bail applications should be heard by the same judge for judicial consistency; Liberty must be balanced against public interest and trial integrity in serious crimes; Allegations of witness tampering must be examined before granting bail

text:
Abdul Mohamed Shaikh @ Abdul Thane vs Union Of India And Anr (Bombay High Court, 2021-05-05). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Regular bail granted after four years of custody; sole reliance on Section 67 NDPS confessions invalid post-Tofan Singh judgment
Summary: Bombay High Court granted bail to a 70-year-old man in an NDPS conspiracy case, holding that prolonged custody without recovery or admissible evidence violated his fundamental rights.
Facts: The applicant, arrested in 2016, was accused in three NDPS cases involving conspiracy to traffic charas. No contraband was recovered from him, and his arrest was based solely on statements recorded under Section 67 of the NDPS Act. Co-accused were granted bail. The trial was pending. The applicant was over 70 years old and had spent more than four years in custody.
Legal issues: Whether statements under Section 67 NDPS Act are admissible as confessions after Tofan Singh judgment; Whether prolonged detention without recovery or corroborative evidence justifies bail; Whether rigour of Section 37 NDPS applies when primary evidence is inadmissible
Reasoning: The court held that in light of the Supreme Court’s Tofan Singh ruling, confessional statements under Section 67 of the NDPS Act are inadmissible. No other evidence was presented against the applicant. With prolonged custody and parity with co-accused already on bail, continued detention violated Article 21 of the Constitution.
Principles: Statements under Section 67 NDPS Act are inadmissible as confessions (Tofan Singh ruling); Prolonged custody without recovery or corroboration violates Article 21; Parity and age are valid grounds for bail in absence of incriminating evidence

Savitri Agarwal & Ors vs State Of Maharashtra & Anr (Supreme Court of India, 2009-07-10). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Anticipatory bail granted by Sessions Court restored by Supreme Court after High Court had cancelled it
Summary: Supreme Court restored anticipatory bail to accused in dowry death case, overturning High Court's cancellation. Emphasized careful application of anticipatory bail principles.
Facts: Laxmi, married to one of the appellants, died from burn injuries along with her infant son. While two dying declarations suggested accidental death, her father alleged dowry harassment. FIR was lodged under Sections 498A, 304B IPC and Sections 3 & 4 Dowry Prohibition Act. Sessions Court granted anticipatory bail; High Court cancelled it; Supreme Court restored it.
Legal issues: Whether anticipatory bail granted by Sessions Court can be cancelled by High Court despite no misuse or non-cooperation by accused; applicability of parameters for anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC.
Reasoning: The Supreme Court held that the Sessions Judge's order was reasoned and not perverse. No evidence of misuse of bail or non-cooperation was found. The High Court had wrongly substituted its discretion without cogent justification. Court reiterated guidelines from Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia case regarding anticipatory bail.
Principles: Anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC need not be time-bound; Distinction between rejection of bail and cancellation of bail; Guidelines from Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia on anticipatory bail

text:
Rahul Dutta vs State Of Haryana (Punjab and Haryana High Court, 2011-12-12). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Regular bail granted after accused challenged his wrongful declaration as proclaimed offender under Section 174-A IPC
Summary: Court held that proclamation under Section 82(4) CrPC is not valid for offences like 498A IPC. Regular bail was granted to accused Rahul Dutta.
Facts: Rahul Dutta, an Australian citizen, was accused by his wife of dowry harassment during their time in Australia. She filed an FIR after returning to India. He was declared a proclaimed offender by the trial court despite arguments that Section 82(4) CrPC was inapplicable for offences like 498A and 406 IPC. He was later arrested and applied for regular bail.
Legal issues: Whether the accused could be legally declared a proclaimed offender under Section 82(4) CrPC for offences not listed therein; validity of proclamation proceedings under CrPC for Section 498A and 406 IPC.
Reasoning: The court ruled that Section 82(4) CrPC applies only to specific IPC sections, which do not include 498A and 406. Thus, declaring the accused a proclaimed offender was legally flawed. Bail was granted since the proclamation was invalid and challan had already been filed.
Principles: Distinction between proclaimed person and proclaimed offender under CrPC; Section 82(4) CrPC applies only to specific IPC offences; Proclaimed offender declaration cannot be made for offences like 498A, 406 IPC

State Of Kadugodi Police, Bangalore vs Gulzar Khan (Karnataka High Court, 1995-08-11). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: High Court upheld anticipatory bail granted by Sessions Court; cancellation plea by State was rejected
Summary: Karnataka High Court upheld anticipatory bail to Gulzar Khan in a murder case, stating cancellation requires strong post-bail misconduct or risk factors.
Facts: Gulzar Khan and others were accused in a murder case involving the stabbing of Thimmaraju. The prosecution cited eye-witnesses including the deceased’s wife and another individual. The Sessions Judge granted anticipatory bail. The State filed for cancellation, alleging misuse of judicial discretion.
Legal issues: Whether anticipatory bail was properly granted when the investigation was still ongoing and the accused was charged with murder under Section 302 IPC.
Reasoning: The High Court held that although the Sessions Judge improperly imported Section 437 standards into anticipatory bail proceedings, the grant was still within judicial discretion. No compelling grounds like tampering with evidence or absconding were shown to justify cancellation.
Principles: Cancellation of anticipatory bail requires cogent and overwhelming circumstances; Section 437 CrPC conditions should not be read into Section 438 CrPC; Inquest report contents not decisive at bail stage

Siddappa S/O. Laxman Naik vs The State Of Karnataka (Karnataka High Court, Dharwad Bench, 2023-05-16). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Regular bail granted to husband in child marriage case after six months of custody; court noted lack of specific assault allegation and consensual cohabitation
Summary: Karnataka High Court granted bail to a man accused under POCSO and child marriage laws, citing lack of specific assault allegation and prolonged custody.
Facts: Siddappa was arrested after marrying a 17-year-old minor who became pregnant. The marriage was arranged under familial pressure. He was charged under IPC Sections 376 and under POCSO and Child Marriage Act. The victim admitted she married under family pressure. There was no specific allegation of sexual assault beyond marital cohabitation. He had been in custody for nearly six months when the High Court granted bail.
Legal issues: Whether regular bail can be granted in a POCSO and child marriage case when cohabitation was under marriage arranged by families and without specific assault allegations.
Reasoning: The Court acknowledged the legal bar on child marriage but considered the consensual nature of marital cohabitation and absence of any overt act or force by the accused. Given the six-month custody and charge sheet being filed, bail was deemed appropriate.
Principles: Bail can be considered even in serious offences if custody is prolonged and no overt act is alleged; Consensual marital cohabitation may be distinguished from sexual assault in child marriage cases; Court must weigh nature of allegations and stage of trial

text:
Usman vs State Of Uttarakhand (Uttarakhand High Court, 2025-03-27). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Regular bail granted due to contradictions in victim’s statements and absence of conclusive medical or CCTV evidence
Summary: Uttarakhand High Court granted bail to Usman in a POCSO case, citing contradictory statements and lack of evidence.
Facts: Usman was accused of abducting and sexually assaulting a minor girl. The FIR was filed two days after the alleged incident, and the victim later made a statement suggesting she implicated Usman out of fear of her father. Medical records and CCTV footage were inconclusive, and there were inconsistencies in her narrative under Section 161 CrPC.
Legal issues: Whether bail should be granted when the victim's statements are contradictory and the medical and CCTV evidence does not corroborate the prosecution's version.
Reasoning: The court observed that contradictions in the victim’s statements and lack of corroborative evidence weakened the prosecution's case. The victim admitted to implicating the accused out of fear. The court found no risk of flight or tampering and granted bail.
Principles: Contradictions in victim statements affect bail decisions; Delay in FIR and absence of medical/CCTV support can favor the accused; Bail is justified when there is no risk of absconding or tampering

text:
State Of Karnataka vs Nagaraja (Karnataka High Court, Bengaluru, 2016-02-23). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: High Court cancelled bail earlier granted to accused by Special Court due to failure to consider victim's statement and seriousness of POCSO charges
Summary: Karnataka High Court cancelled bail in a POCSO case, finding the lower court ignored key evidence and the gravity of the offense.
Facts: The accused Nagaraja was charged with abducting and sexually assaulting a 17-year-old girl with the help of a co-accused. He allegedly raped her after forcibly taking her in an autorickshaw, and she later attempted suicide. The Sessions Court granted him bail citing custody duration and his family role. The State sought cancellation citing ignored evidence including the victim's statement under Section 164 CrPC.
Legal issues: Whether bail can be cancelled when earlier bail was granted without properly considering the victim's statement and the seriousness of POCSO allegations.
Reasoning: The High Court found that the Special Judge failed to apply judicial mind and overlooked critical materials like the victim's 164 CrPC statement and the presumption under Section 29 of the POCSO Act. Bail was granted based on weak reasoning such as custody duration, and not on the merits or seriousness of the case.
Principles: Courts must provide cogent reasons when granting bail in serious offences; Victim's statement under Section 164 CrPC must be considered; Presumption under Section 29 of the POCSO Act applies post-charge sheet; Bail once granted can be cancelled if it was done without due consideration of material facts

Prakash S/O Mahaveer Shiragavankar vs The State Of Karnataka (Karnataka High Court, Dharwad Bench, 2022-11-16). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Successive bail petition by accused in POCSO gang rape case rejected due to lack of changed circumstances and serious allegations of gang rape of minor
Summary: High Court rejected successive bail plea of accused in a POCSO gang rape case, citing no change in circumstances and serious charges.
Facts: The petitioner, accused no. 3, was arrested along with others for abducting and gang-raping a minor girl. The incident involved confinement and repeated sexual assault by multiple accused. The prior bail application had been rejected. Accused no. 1 later committed suicide in jail. The petitioner filed a fresh bail plea shortly after, citing no new material changes.
Legal issues: Whether successive bail can be granted in a gang rape case involving a minor under POCSO when no significant change in circumstances is shown.
Reasoning: The court held that the previous detailed bail rejection order already addressed all contentions. There was no new evidence or legal change except the suicide of co-accused. Given the seriousness of allegations, including repeat gang rape and abduction of a minor, bail was denied.
Principles: Successive bail requires significant change in circumstances; Gang rape of a minor under POCSO is a grave offense with life imprisonment; Courts must prioritize victim protection and witness safety in such cases

text:
Nilam Khatoon vs The State Of Bihar (Patna High Court, 2024-04-03). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Regular bail granted to woman accused of trafficking and sexual exploitation, citing custodial period and parity with co-accused
Summary: Patna High Court granted bail to Nilam Khatoon in a trafficking case, noting her custody and parity with co-accused.
Facts: Based on NGO information, police raided a house and found minors allegedly trafficked for sexual exploitation. Nilam Khatoon was found in one room with a girl who stated the petitioner assaulted her and forced her into sexual activity. Condoms were recovered from the scene. The petitioner claimed innocence and cited absence of direct recovery from her and bail to similarly placed co-accused.
Legal issues: Whether regular bail should be granted in a human trafficking and sexual exploitation case when the accused is a woman, in prolonged custody, and co-accused have been granted bail.
Reasoning: The court considered the petitioner’s gender, lack of criminal antecedents, and prolonged custody since September 2023. Bail was granted with conditions, following the principle of parity with a similarly situated co-accused.
Principles: Parity with similarly situated co-accused; Prolonged custody as ground for bail; Bail to female accused in absence of direct recovery

text:
Khundongbam Joychandra Meitei vs The Officer-In-Charge (Manipur High Court, 2022-10-10). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Anticipatory bail rejected in case of alleged forced elopement and repeated sexual assault under false pretext of marriage
Summary: Manipur High Court denied anticipatory bail to accused in rape case involving forced elopement and fake court marriage with a differently-abled woman.
Facts: The petitioner was in a long-term relationship with the complainant, a differently-abled woman. She alleged he abducted her, staged a fake court marriage, and sexually assaulted her multiple times under the pretext of marriage. After their relationship ended, he began a new relationship, prompting her to file an FIR. The petitioner sought anticipatory bail fearing arrest.
Legal issues: Whether anticipatory bail can be granted when sexual relations are alleged to have occurred under false promise of marriage, compounded by elements of force, fraud, and the victim’s disability.
Reasoning: The court found prima facie evidence that the petitioner kidnapped and repeatedly raped the victim under false pretenses of marriage. The court emphasized the seriousness of the offense, the need for custodial interrogation, and that such actions constitute crimes against women. Cited that anticipatory bail is not justified in such grave matters.
Principles: False promise to marry may vitiate consent under Section 375 IPC; Custodial interrogation is necessary in serious cases involving fraud and rape; Anticipatory bail is not justified where prima facie offence of rape and cheating is made out

Huligeppa S/O Shivalingappa Vaddar vs The State Of Karnataka (Karnataka High Court, Dharwad Bench, 2022-11-16). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Successive bail petition rejected in POCSO case involving minor, citing prior similar offense and risk of reoffending
Summary: Karnataka High Court denied bail to accused in POCSO case citing seriousness of charges, victim’s minority, and petitioner’s prior similar case.
Facts: The petitioner was arrested for allegedly having sexual intercourse with a minor girl who stayed with him for several days. Despite claiming consensual relation, the victim was a minor under POCSO. FSL report showed no biological evidence, but medical report confirmed old hymen tear. The petitioner had a prior similar case where he was acquitted as the victim turned hostile.
Legal issues: Whether regular bail can be granted to a repeat offender accused under POCSO when medical evidence supports victim's statement and FSL is inconclusive.
Reasoning: The Court rejected bail citing the minor’s age, the seriousness of the offense under POCSO, and the petitioner’s history of a similar prior case. Despite lack of forensic confirmation due to time lapse, medical findings supported sexual assault. Granting bail posed a risk of reoffending and tampering with evidence.
Principles: Consent is immaterial for victims under 18 in POCSO cases; Prior acquittal in similar case indicates habitual pattern despite lack of conviction; Medical evidence can outweigh absence of forensic stains if time has lapsed

text:
Morasiya Kalubhai Rambhai vs State Of Gujarat (Gujarat High Court, 2022-05-19). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Anticipatory bail granted with stringent conditions despite serious POCSO and IPC charges, considering cooperation and legal precedent
Summary: Gujarat High Court granted anticipatory bail to accused in POCSO case, citing legal precedent and absence of need for custodial interrogation.
Facts: The applicant was accused under IPC and POCSO sections for allegedly sexually assaulting a minor. The FIR included grave charges, but the defense argued the accused was cooperating and posed no flight risk. The court considered legal precedent and imposed multiple conditions while granting anticipatory bail.
Legal issues: Whether anticipatory bail can be granted in serious POCSO cases based on cooperation, lack of custodial necessity, and legal precedent.
Reasoning: Despite opposition from the prosecution, the court relied on principles from Siddharam Satlingappa Mhetre and Gurubaksh Singh Sibbia cases, concluding that custodial interrogation was unnecessary. Anticipatory bail was granted with detailed compliance conditions.
Principles: Anticipatory bail can be granted even in serious offences if custodial interrogation is not required; Court must evaluate cooperation and risk of tampering; Guidelines from Siddharam Satlingappa Mhetre and Gurubaksh Singh Sibbia apply

text:
Brahmprakash @ Brhamprakash Dalchand vs State Of Gujarat (Gujarat High Court, 2021-04-20). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Anticipatory bail granted to railway official in sexual harassment case, considering lack of evidentiary support in internal inquiry and applicant’s seniority
Summary: Gujarat High Court granted anticipatory bail to senior railway official accused of sexual harassment, citing lack of supporting evidence and applicant’s clean record.
Facts: The complainant, a female railway doctor, alleged that her superior, the applicant, sexually harassed her at the workplace with offensive remarks and misconduct. An internal committee dismissed the complaint for lack of evidentiary support. The defense claimed the complaint was retaliatory due to a transfer and emphasized the applicant’s unblemished record. The High Court granted anticipatory bail citing lack of prima facie evidence and legal precedents.
Legal issues: Whether anticipatory bail can be granted in a workplace sexual harassment case where internal inquiry finds no substance in the allegations and the accused has no prior record.
Reasoning: The Court found that the internal complaints committee’s inquiry did not support the allegations, and the complainant’s FIR appeared to be an improved version of earlier submissions. Considering the applicant’s age, service record, and absence of clear evidence, anticipatory bail was deemed appropriate.
Principles: Anticipatory bail permissible where internal inquiry shows no evidentiary basis; Observations from Internal Complaint Committee may influence bail decision; Siddharam Satlingappa Mhetre and Gurubaksh Singh Sibbia principles considered

Outcome detail: Bail consideration deferred after informant contested disclosure on accused’s prior criminal history; court awaits affidavit clarifying antecedents
Summary: Patna High Court deferred decision on bail for accused in sexual offense case due to disputed antecedents and need for further clarification via affidavit.
Facts: The accused, Shambhu Pandey, was arrested in connection with a case involving allegations of attempt to rape and murder under IPC and POCSO provisions. Summary: Gauhati High Court denied anticipatory bail to Ali Hussain in a POCSO case, citing credible minor victim's statement and seriousness of offense.
Facts: Ali Hussain sought pre-arrest bail in a case where he was accused of sexually abusing a minor girl. The victim, in her Section 164 CrPC statement, directly implicated him. Legal issues: Whether anticipatory bail can be granted in a POCSO case where the victim has clearly implicated the accused and is a minor.
Reasoning: The Court held that minor's consent is not a defense under POCSO and a prima facie case existed against the accused based on the victim’s testimony. Outcome detail: Suspension of sentence and interim bail during appeal rejected in POCSO conviction case involving 12-year-old differently abled victim
Summary: Bombay High Court denied interim bail during appeal to man convicted of raping a 12-year-old differently abled girl, citing seriousness of offense.
Facts: Bharat Budha Koli, convicted under Section 376(1) IPC and Section 6 of the POCSO Act for raping a 12-year-old differently abled girl, sought suspension of sentence and bail during the pendency of his appeal. Legal issues: Whether sentence can be suspended and bail granted during appeal in a serious POCSO conviction involving a minor and differently abled child.
Reasoning: The court found that the nature of the offense--rape of a minor who was also differently abled--was too grave to merit bail even during appeal, despite the petitioner already serving five years. The evidence from nine witnesses and medical support were considered sufficient to uphold the seriousness.
Principles: Suspension of sentence during appeal may be denied in serious POCSO offenses; Length of incarceration alone not sufficient for bail post-conviction; Special protection under POCSO for differently abled minors increases gravity

Talib vs State Of U.P. And 3 Others (High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, 2022-05-16). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Regular bail granted due to contradictions in victim's statements and no injury found on medical exam
Summary: Bail granted to youth accused in POCSO case, citing contradictions in victim's testimony and absence of injuries.
Facts: The applicant was accused of kidnapping and sexually assaulting a 17-year-old girl. The victim traveled with the applicant across cities and lived with him for about four months. Contradictions were found between her statements under Sections 161 and 164 CrPC, and her medical examination showed no injuries. The applicant had no prior criminal record.
Legal issues: Whether bail should be granted in a POCSO case involving a minor where the victim resided with the accused voluntarily and inconsistencies exist in her testimony.
Reasoning: The Court noted the applicant's age (19), the victim's age (17 years, 7 months), prolonged cohabitation, contradictions in her statements, and clean criminal record. These factors justified granting bail.

text:
Rhea Chakraborty vs Union Of India And Anr (Bombay High Court, 2020-10-07). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Regular bail granted despite NDPS charges; court ruled Section 27A not applicable based on evidence, and emphasized reformative approach
Summary: Bombay High Court granted bail to Rhea Chakraborty, rejecting NCB's claim under Section 27A NDPS and citing lack of evidence for financing or harbouring.
Facts: Rhea Chakraborty was arrested under multiple NDPS Act sections for allegedly procuring and financing drug use for Sushant Singh Rajput. NCB alleged she facilitated and financed drug procurement via intermediaries. Her bail plea was earlier rejected by Special Court citing Section 27A, but the High Court found no material showing her active involvement in drug trafficking or harbouring under Section 27A.
Legal issues: Whether Section 27A NDPS applies to accused when contraband is not recovered and role is limited to alleged procurement for another's consumption.
Reasoning: The Court held that there was no material suggesting the accused financed illicit trafficking or harboured a drug offender under Section 27A. It emphasized the reformative aspect of NDPS Act and found that bail conditions under Section 37 were not triggered in her case.
Principles: All NDPS offenses are non-bailable unless explicitly bailable under CrPC Schedule; Section 27A requires specific material on financing illicit trafficking or harbouring; Section 37 NDPS bail limitations are triggered only in serious categories including 19, 24, 27A and commercial quantity offenses; Statements under Section 67 NDPS Act are not conclusive for denial of bail if retracted and unsupported by evidence; Reformative approach under NDPS Act must guide bail decisions in cases not involving commercial quantity

text:
Navinkumar Pandu Jatot vs The State Of Maharashtra (Bombay High Court, 2022-01-31). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Bail granted under Section 167(2) CrPC due to incomplete charge sheet lacking CA report within 180 days in NDPS case
Summary: Bombay High Court granted default bail in NDPS case due to non-filing of CA report with charge sheet within 180 days, holding it incomplete.
Facts: Navinkumar Pandu Jatot and others were arrested with 41.1 kg of ganja in a vehicle. The charge sheet was filed within 180 days but without the CA (Chemical Analyzer) report. The accused claimed default bail under Section 167(2) CrPC, arguing the charge sheet was incomplete under NDPS Act.
Legal issues: Whether a charge sheet under NDPS Act filed without the Chemical Analyzer’s report constitutes an incomplete charge sheet entitling the accused to default bail under Section 167(2) CrPC.
Reasoning: The Court held that the charge sheet filed without the CA report is incomplete in light of precedents where such omission was considered critical in narcotics cases. It ruled that the accused had an accrued right to default bail since the report was not filed within 180 days and no extension was sought.
Principles: A charge sheet filed without the CA report in NDPS cases is incomplete and entitles the accused to default bail under Section 167(2) CrPC; The CA report is a vital document in narcotics cases and its absence renders the charge sheet inadequate for cognizance; Failure to file CA report within 180 days without seeking extension under Section 36-A(4) NDPS Act results in default bail

Shreyas Dike And Ors vs The State Of Maharashtra (Bombay High Court, 2018-12-13). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Bail applications rejected for all accused due to serious and repeated sexual assault allegations against a minor
Summary: Bail was denied to all accused in a case involving repeated sexual assaults on a minor, citing detailed allegations and seriousness of the offense.
Facts: A 15-year-old girl was repeatedly raped and sexually assaulted by multiple accused between May 2017 and January 2018. The assaults were committed under threats involving a video. The FIR was filed on 3rd February 2018. The accused were arrested shortly thereafter. The complainant named each accused and provided detailed instances of assault.
Legal issues: Whether the bail can be granted in a case involving repeated sexual assault of a minor; whether delay in lodging FIR affects credibility.
Reasoning: Given the minor status of the victim, detailed and specific allegations, and repeated nature of sexual abuse under coercion, the court found no reason to disbelieve the FIR and held that the matter of delay and lack of medical evidence were trial matters.

text:
Sunil Mahadev Patil vs The State Of Maharashtra (Bombay High Court, 2015-08-03). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Bail granted due to mitigating circumstances including consensual elopement and absence of violence
Summary: Bail granted to a 20-year-old accused in a sexual offense case involving consensual elopement with a 15-year-old, with the court considering mitigating factors.
Facts: The accused and the 15-year-old prosecutrix were in a romantic relationship. On 25th November 2014, they eloped, allegedly married in a temple, and stayed together until being found on 9th December 2014. The accused was arrested and charged under IPC and POCSO sections. The prosecution claimed kidnapping and rape; the defense argued consensual elopement.
Legal issues: Whether bail can be granted when a minor elopes with the accused due to mutual affection and no violence is alleged.
Reasoning: The court recognized that though the girl was a minor and consent legally immaterial, the relationship appeared consensual, non-violent, and involved an informal marriage. Considering the accused’s young age, lack of antecedents, and no threat of coercion, bail was granted with conditions.

text:
Milind Ravindra Hindurao vs The State Of Maharashtra And Anr (Bombay High Court, 2021-04-08). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Pre-arrest bail granted after court found no prima facie case under Atrocities Act or IPC Section 376
Summary: Bombay High Court granted anticipatory bail to a police constable accused of rape and caste-based harassment, citing lack of prima facie case under SC/ST Act and consensual nature of relationship.
Facts: The complainant, a student and political youth leader, alleged that the accused, a police constable, developed a relationship with her under the promise of marriage and later sexually assaulted her. An FIR was registered under IPC Sections 376, 420, 506 and provisions of the Atrocities Act. The accused sought anticipatory bail after a Sessions Court rejected it.
Legal issues: Whether anticipatory bail is barred under Section 18 of the Atrocities Act when no prima facie case is made out; whether allegations support charges under IPC Section 376.
Reasoning: The court found significant delay in reporting the alleged incidents and discrepancies in earlier complaints. WhatsApp chats indicated consensual relationship. The court held that no prima facie case under the Atrocities Act or Section 376 IPC was made out, allowing anticipatory bail with conditions.

Prashant Suryakant Date vs The State Of Maharashtra (Bombay High Court, 2021-02-15). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Bail granted after court found discrepancies and delay in reporting, and absence of medical evidence of sexual assault
Summary: Bombay High Court granted regular bail in a POCSO and IPC 377 case citing delay, lack of medical evidence, and discrepancies in victim's statements.
Facts: The victim, a 17-year-old boy, was allegedly sexually assaulted by the accused, a relative, during a week-long stay at his house in June 2020. The FIR was filed over a month later, after a family dispute. Medical reports showed no evidence of assault.
Legal issues: Whether delay in filing FIR and absence of medical evidence can cast doubt on allegations under IPC Section 377 and POCSO Act.
Reasoning: The court noted inconsistencies in the victim's statements, delayed reporting of the incident, prior enmity between parties, and lack of medical evidence. These raised doubts about the prosecution’s case, justifying bail.

text:
Faiz Rehman vs State Of Odisha (Orissa High Court, 2019-08-21). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Second successive bail application rejected due to potential tampering with evidence and no change in circumstances
Summary: Orissa High Court rejected the second bail plea of a shelter chairman accused of sexually abusing girls, citing unchanged circumstances and pending witness examination.
Facts: Faiz Rehman, Chairman of an unregistered child shelter, was accused of sexually abusing several girl inmates over years. An FIR was lodged following a complaint by the Child Welfare Committee based on reports by the children. The charge sheet included IPC and POCSO Act violations. Some victims turned hostile, but others remained to be examined.
Legal issues: Whether bail should be granted when some victims have turned hostile, and whether any change in circumstance justifies a successive bail application.
Reasoning: The court denied bail citing lack of changed circumstances, pending examination of key witnesses, the influential position of the accused, and potential risk of evidence tampering. Prior rejection was reaffirmed based on seriousness of accusations and societal impact.

text:
Mrs Bratati @ Pinky vs The State Of Karnataka (Karnataka High Court, 2019-08-20). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Bail previously granted not cancelled; court found no violation of bail conditions and dismissed cancellation plea
Summary: Karnataka High Court dismissed a plea to cancel bail in a POCSO case, ruling that no post-bail violations occurred and procedural changes could not be applied retrospectively.
Facts: The petitioner sought cancellation of bail granted to her husband, the accused, in a case involving charges of rape and sexual assault on their daughter. The petitioner alleged pre-bail threats, procedural violations, and misuse of judicial process. The court noted no post-bail violations and dismissed the cancellation petition.
Legal issues: Whether bail granted can be cancelled due to alleged threats prior to bail and whether procedural non-compliance under Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2018 justifies cancellation.
Reasoning: The court held that the accused had not violated bail conditions post-release, and alleged threats occurred before bail. It rejected the retrospective application of the 2018 Amendment and found no grounds for cancellation.

text:
Razak Hussain vs UT of J&K Through SHO (High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh at Jammu, 2023-09-29). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Interim bail for accused Nos. 4 and 5 (Waseem Akram and Sahil Choudhary) revoked due to addition of gang rape charges under Section 376D IPC.
Summary: Anticipatory bail for two accused was revoked after gang rape allegations surfaced during investigation. The court deemed the charges serious enough to deny bail.
Facts: The petitioners, including Waseem Akram and Sahil Choudhary, sought anticipatory bail in relation to FIR No. 351/2021 for offenses including cruelty and later gang rape. The complainant alleged severe mistreatment and sexual abuse by her in-laws and an unidentified tantrik. Her statement under Section 164 CrPC led to the addition of Section 376D IPC. Interim bail was granted earlier but later challenged.
Legal issues: Whether interim bail should be revoked after the addition of gang rape charges under Section 376D IPC during investigation.
Reasoning: The Court found that the allegations of gang rape, reiterated in the complainant's statement under Section 164 CrPC, constituted supervening developments justifying revocation of interim bail. It held that FIR need not be exhaustive and that serious offenses revealed during investigation warrant denial of anticipatory bail.

text:
Yeshappa Mundalmani @ Yesuraj vs The State Of Karnataka And Anr (High Court of Karnataka, Kalaburagi Bench, 2023-10-26). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Regular bail rejected due to serious nature of offence and active abetment in recording sexual assault on a minor.
Summary: Bail was denied to the accused who allegedly recorded and abetted the sexual assault of a minor. Court held the offence as grave under POCSO and I.T. Act.
Facts: The petitioner, accused No.3, allegedly videographed the sexual assault of a 14-year-old girl by accused No.1 and helped circulate the video. The victim was coerced by accused No.1 into accompanying him, and the assault was recorded and later shared. The petitioner was arrested and remained in judicial custody for over 6 months before applying for bail.
Legal issues: Whether the petitioner’s act of videographing and abetting a sexual assault on a minor amounts to a grave offence under POCSO and I.T. Acts, justifying denial of bail.
Reasoning: The court held that the petitioner’s role in abetting the assault by recording and sharing the act constituted a serious offence under Section 67(B) of the I.T. Act and Section 17 of POCSO. Granting bail could risk tampering with evidence and witnesses, especially since prior threats had been made.

text:
Ashoka vs State Of Karnataka (High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru, 2022-11-03). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Regular bail granted; prior rejection order set aside due to inconsistencies in victim’s statements and DNA report excluding accused as biological father.
Summary: Bail granted to the accused in a POCSO case due to conflicting evidence and a DNA report negating paternity. Court found no prima facie case against the accused.
Facts: The accused, Ashoka, was charged with raping a minor girl, leading to her pregnancy and childbirth. Conflicting statements were made by the victim, implicating both Ashoka and another person named Ananda. A DNA report excluded Ashoka as the biological father, and surprisingly, also indicated the girl was not the biological mother. The trial court had earlier denied bail.
Legal issues: Whether inconsistent victim statements and exculpatory DNA evidence negate the prima facie case required to deny bail.
Reasoning: The court found that inconsistencies in the victim’s statements and the DNA report failing to establish paternity created doubt over the prosecution’s case. It criticized the lower court for overlooking these facts and held that bail should not be denied if a prima facie case does not exist.

Reasoning: The High Court found that the Special Judge exercised discretion appropriately, recorded reasons, and there was no post-bail misconduct or violation of conditions by the accused. Therefore, the court declined to cancel the bail.

text:
Pokar Ram vs State Of Rajasthan And Anr (Supreme Court of India, 1985-04-17). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Anticipatory bail cancelled by Supreme Court due to lack of justification by Sessions Court
Summary: Supreme Court cancelled anticipatory bail granted to Chandan Singh in a murder case, finding the Sessions Court had erred in law and failed to apply proper legal standards.
Facts: On August 23, 1983, Bhanwaria, son of the appellant, was shot and later died of injuries. The FIR implicated Chandan Singh. Despite serious allegations, the Sessions Court granted anticipatory bail. The complainant challenged the order.
Legal issues: Whether anticipatory bail can be granted in a murder case without proper judicial reasoning; scope of High Court’s and Sessions Court’s discretion in anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC.
Reasoning: The Supreme Court held that anticipatory bail in a serious case like murder must be granted only with compelling reasons. The Sessions Judge failed to record relevant considerations, and thus anticipatory bail was improperly granted.
Principles: Anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC requires strong justification, especially in grave offences; Distinction between anticipatory and post-arrest bail; Public faith in justice system may be eroded by unjustified pre-arrest bail

Reasoning: The court found that the grant of interim bail was in violation of CrPC Section 439(1A) and Practice Directions requiring notice to complainants in sexual offense cases. The interim bail order was set aside, and specific compliance instructions were reiterated.
Principles: Mandatory notice to complainant before bail under IPC 376/POCSO; Procedural compliance under Section 439(1A) CrPC and High Court Practice Directions; Victim’s right to be heard in bail proceedings in sexual offense cases

text:
Charakonda Chinna Chennaiah vs The State Of Telangana (Telangana High Court, 2021-02-23). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Preventive detention order quashed; regular bail granted earlier was not violated
Summary: Telangana High Court quashed the preventive detention order against an accused in a POCSO case, ruling that a single incident does not justify invoking preventive detention laws.
Facts: The petitioner challenged the preventive detention order against his son, who was accused of sexually assaulting a 13-year-old girl. The boy had been released on bail and had no prior criminal history. The detention order was based solely on this one FIR and alleged future risk to public order.
Legal issues: Whether preventive detention is justified based on a single incident of sexual offense, and whether such offense constitutes a threat to public order or merely law and order.
Reasoning: The court held that a single incident, without any evidence of repeated conduct or bail condition violation, does not justify preventive detention. The offense, while grave, fell under 'law and order' and not 'public order'. Hence, detention was unwarranted.

Kotari Amboji vs State Of Telangana (Telangana High Court, 2022-07-18). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Preventive detention order quashed; regular bail in solitary POCSO case was not a ground to invoke preventive detention
Summary: Telangana High Court quashed preventive detention of a man accused under POCSO, stating that a single case did not warrant invoking preventive detention for public order concerns.
Facts: The accused, Kotari Amboji, was booked under IPC Section 376AB and POCSO Act for sexually assaulting a five-year-old girl. He was granted regular bail by the Special Court. Subsequently, a preventive detention order was issued by the state citing public order concerns. The accused challenged the detention order in a writ petition.
Legal issues: Whether a solitary POCSO case justifies preventive detention for disturbing public order, despite the accused being out on regular bail and facing criminal prosecution.
Reasoning: The High Court held that the act, though heinous, did not constitute a public order disturbance and fell under law and order. It emphasized that preventive detention cannot substitute regular criminal prosecution and quashed the detention order.
Principles: Distinction between law and order and public order; Preventive detention should not substitute regular prosecution under IPC and POCSO

Outcome detail: Bail granted by Additional Sessions Judge after illegal detention; High Court found manipulation of records by SDM
Summary: Madhya Pradesh High Court ruled that the SDM had unlawfully detained advocate Durgalal Vijay despite a bail order, manipulated court records, and awarded compensation for the illegal detention.
Facts: Durgalal Vijay was arrested after an altercation with an official. He was granted bail by the Magistrate but was not released, and subsequently re-arrested under Section 151 CrPC. The SDM allegedly manipulated court records to show rejection of bail and extended illegal detention. The High Court found gross misconduct and awarded compensation.
Legal issues: Whether detention under Section 151 CrPC after bail for a substantive offense is legal; whether SDM can manipulate judicial records and detain accused without authority.
Reasoning: The Court held that the SDM acted with mala fide intent, exceeded his jurisdiction, manipulated court records, and detained the petitioner unlawfully even after bail was granted. It directed compensation and disciplinary action.
Principles: Illegal detention and compensation for violation of Article 21; Magistrate’s jurisdiction under Section 151 CrPC; Judicial accountability and manipulation of records

text:
G.S. Jhaj vs State Of Punjab (Punjab and Haryana High Court, 2001-03-29). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Bail granted by judicial officer in NDPS matter without noting prior rejection; became basis for assessing officer's doubtful integrity
Summary: Punjab and Haryana High Court upheld the compulsory retirement of a judicial officer who granted bail in an NDPS case without explaining deviation from earlier rejection, citing concerns over judicial integrity.
Facts: While posted as a judge, G.S. Jhaj granted bail in an NDPS matter involving 3 kg of opium, ignoring the fact that an earlier bail application had been rejected by another judge. No reasons were recorded for deviating from the earlier decision. A second accused was denied bail shortly after. These contradictory orders led to questions about the officer’s integrity and his compulsory retirement.
Legal issues: Whether a judicial officer’s integrity can be questioned based on inconsistent bail orders in related narcotics cases and whether such assessment can justify compulsory retirement without formal inquiry.
Reasoning: The Court held that conflicting bail decisions in connected cases without explanation raised reasonable suspicion of lack of integrity. The order of compulsory retirement was justified based on these facts and was not punitive but in public interest.
Principles: Compulsory retirement in public interest does not require formal inquiry; Judicial integrity can be assessed from conduct in bail matters; Conflicting judicial decisions without reasons may indicate misconduct

text:
Gaurav Kumar @ Lakha @ Gaurav Thakur vs The State Of Bihar (Patna High Court, 2019-09-30). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Bail rejected by Children's Court; High Court addressed legal questions around bail rights of juveniles in heinous offenses under the 2015 JJ Act
Summary: Patna High Court clarified important legal questions on bail for juveniles between 16–18 years in heinous offense cases. The accused’s bail was rejected, but the ruling emphasized a child-rights-focused interpretation of the JJ Act.
Facts: Gaurav Kumar, aged 17 years at the time of the offense, was accused under Section 302 IPC in Buxar PS Case No. 236/2018. The Juvenile Justice Board determined his age and referred him for trial as an adult. His bail application before the Children's Court was rejected, leading to an appeal under Section 101(5) of the JJ Act.
Legal issues: Whether a juvenile between 16-18 years can seek bail during or after preliminary assessment; whether the Children's Court must follow CrPC or JJ Act in bail matters; whether seriousness of offense alone justifies bail denial.
Reasoning: The Court undertook a detailed legal analysis of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, focusing on Section 12, and held that bail should not be denied solely on the ground of offense seriousness. However, due to statutory nuances and procedural history, the specific appeal was not allowed.
Principles: Bail rights of juveniles aged 16-18 in heinous offenses; Interpretation of Section 12 and 101(5) of JJ Act, 2015; Primacy of Juvenile Justice principles over CrPC in bail matters involving children

text:
Hemu Pant @ Hemu Kalu & Another vs State Of Uttarakhand (Uttarakhand High Court, 2015-06-23). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Bail rejected due to conflicting opinions and lack of parity grounds with co-accused whose bail was granted by different bench
Summary: Uttarakhand High Court ruled that subsequent bail applications must go before the same bench that previously rejected bail, and declined Hemu Pant’s plea based on co-accused parity.
Facts: Hemu Pant and Manish were convicted under Sections 302, 364, and 201 IPC. While Manish was later granted bail during appeal, Hemu’s subsequent applications were rejected due to legal conflict over whether parity applied and which bench had jurisdiction to decide repeated bail pleas. The matter was escalated to a Full Bench for resolution.
Legal issues: Whether a subsequent bail application during appeal should be heard by the same bench which rejected earlier bail, and whether parity with a co-accused granted bail by another bench is valid grounds for bail.
Reasoning: The Full Bench held that subsequent bail applications must be heard by the same bench that rejected prior ones unless reassigned by the Chief Justice, emphasizing judicial discipline and consistency. Parity alone was found insufficient when earlier applications had been rejected on merit.
Principles: Subsequent bail application must go before same bench that rejected prior bail; Chief Justice controls roster and bench assignments; Parity not sufficient when earlier application rejected on merits

Lalu Kumar @ Lal Babu @ Lallu vs The State Of Bihar (Patna High Court, 2019-10-01). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Bail rejected by Children's Court and the High Court deliberated on maintainability and procedure under Juvenile Justice Act
Summary: Court ruled that bail applications for juveniles accused of heinous offenses must follow the JJ Act, not CrPC. Seriousness of offense alone is not sufficient ground to deny bail.
Facts: Lalu Kumar, aged 17, was accused in a murder case (IPC 302) and taken into custody. The Juvenile Justice Board assessed him and ordered trial as an adult due to the heinous nature of the offense. His bail application before the Children's Court was rejected. He challenged the order under Section 101(5) of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015.
Legal issues: Whether a child aged 16–18 accused of heinous offense can apply for bail before preliminary assessment; Whether Children's Court can entertain bail applications and on what basis; Whether seriousness of offense alone can justify denial of bail to a juvenile; Whether appeal under Section 101(5) of JJ Act is maintainable against bail rejection
Reasoning: The court held that bail to juveniles must be governed by the Juvenile Justice Act and not CrPC; seriousness of the offense alone cannot justify denial. It also clarified jurisdictional and procedural aspects regarding bail applications and appeals under the JJ Act.
Principles: Children aged 16–18 accused of heinous offenses may be tried as adults under JJ Act, 2015; Bail must be considered per Section 12 JJ Act and not CrPC; Appeals against Children's Court bail orders maintainable under Section 101(5) JJ Act

Lokesh Sharma S/O Gopal Krishan vs Union Of India And Ors (Bombay High Court, 2019-06-14). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Bail rejected for accused Lokesh Sharma and others due to prima facie evidence suggesting involvement in Malegaon blast
Summary: Bail was denied to Lokesh Sharma and co-accused in the 2006 Malegaon blasts case. The court found sufficient prima facie evidence presented by the NIA.
Facts: On 8 September 2006, four bombs exploded in Malegaon, Maharashtra, killing 31 and injuring over 300. Initially, ATS and CBI investigated the case, charging members of a different group. Later, NIA took over and filed a supplementary chargesheet against Lokesh Sharma and others, alleging a different conspiracy.
Legal issues: Whether the accused are entitled to bail under Section 43D(5) of the UAPA given prima facie evidence presented by NIA.
Reasoning: The court held that the materials including confessions, test identification parade, recovery of bicycle parts, and training camp evidence provided reasonable grounds for believing the accusations were prima facie true under Section 43D(5) of the UAPA. Hence, bail was denied.

Outcome detail: Bail applications rejected by Special Judge under NIA Act; upheld by High Court
Summary: Bail was denied to the accused Manohar Narwaria in the Malegaon blast case. The court upheld the NIA's evidence and rejected the bail plea citing UAPA restrictions.
Facts: On 8th September 2006, four bomb explosions occurred in Malegaon, Maharashtra, killing 31 and injuring over 300. The initial investigation blamed members of SIMI. Later, the NIA reinvestigated and charged a different set of accused, including the appellant, alleging a Hindu extremist conspiracy.
Legal issues: Whether the accused could be granted bail under UAPA given the prima facie material and delay in trial; whether NIA's findings could override ATS and CBI charge sheets.
Reasoning: The court held that there were reasonable grounds to believe the accusations against the appellant were prima facie true under Section 43D(5) of the UAPA, based on witness testimonies, discovery of bomb planting sites, and identification in TIP. Long pre-trial detention alone was not enough to grant bail under UAPA provisions.

Mohd. Khalid vs State Of UP (High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench, 2018-03-27). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Regular bail rejected due to prima facie evidence of arms trafficking and connections with anti-national activities
Summary: Bail application of Mohd. Khalid was rejected based on strong evidence of illegal arms trade and connections with anti-national elements. Court cited the risk of tampering with evidence and public interest.
Facts: The accused, Mohd. Khalid, was arrested on 17.04.2013 for illegal arms possession. Recovery included multiple pistols, foreign arms parts, and forged licenses. The investigation revealed links with multiple co-accused, and sales of illegal arms to anti-national groups. He was managing National Gun House illegally and was found to have deposited large sums in accounts linked to co-accused involved in arms smuggling.
Legal issues: Whether the accused's alleged involvement in illegal arms trade and links with anti-national elements justify denial of bail under serious IPC sections including 121A and 122.
Reasoning: The court found substantial material evidence including recovery memos, call records, forensic reports, and witness statements linking the accused to a larger arms trafficking network. Bail was denied due to seriousness of the offenses and risk of tampering with evidence.

text:
Nanha S/O Nabhan Kha vs State Of U.P. (Allahabad High Court, 1992-09-18). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Third bail application rejected; court held that parity alone is not sufficient ground for bail without assessing individual case merits
Summary: The court rejected the third bail application of the accused, holding that parity alone cannot justify bail. Each case must be individually evaluated even in subsequent applications.
Facts: The accused, Nanha, was booked along with three co-accused under Section 302 IPC. Earlier bail applications of Nanha and some co-accused were rejected. Some co-accused were later granted bail. Nanha filed a third bail application claiming parity with the co-accused.
Legal issues: Whether an accused is entitled to bail on the ground of parity in a second or third bail application when a co-accused has been subsequently granted bail without disclosing earlier rejection of others’ bail applications.
Reasoning: The court held that parity alone is not a sufficient ground for bail. Each bail application must be considered on its individual merits, taking into account the role of the accused, the stage of the case, and the broader principles of justice. While consistency is desirable, exceptions exist based on facts and judicial discretion.
Principles: Parity alone is not a sufficient ground for bail; Judicial consistency is desirable but not absolute in bail matters; Each bail application must be evaluated independently on its merits

text:
Nirmil Jitendrabhai Shah vs State Of Gujarat (Gujarat High Court, 2024-04-05). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Anticipatory bail cancelled due to abuse of process and no substantial change in circumstances
Summary: The Gujarat High Court cancelled anticipatory bail granted to an accused in a property fraud case. The Court ruled that no substantial change in circumstances existed to justify a successive bail application.
Facts: The complainant, Nirmil Shah, purchased a property in Ahmedabad in 2018. His wife, suffering from a psychological disorder, allegedly sold the property using a forged power of attorney. The accused, Karan Devendrabhai Rabari, was the beneficiary of this forged sale deed. Multiple FIRs were filed, including for criminal trespass and forgery. Anticipatory bail granted earlier to the accused was challenged by the complainant.
Legal issues: Whether successive anticipatory bail can be granted without substantial change in circumstances; whether principle of parity applies when co-accused are granted bail; whether fraud in sale of property warrants cancellation of anticipatory bail.
Reasoning: The Court found that the Sessions Court erred in granting successive anticipatory bail based only on parity and without any real change in circumstances. The forged power of attorney and fraudulent sale deed constituted serious offences. The accused had prior criminal antecedents and had evaded investigation.

Summary: Madhya Pradesh High Court granted bail to a rape accused after the victim and her mother retracted their allegations. The Court noted the prolonged custody and lack of supporting evidence.
Facts: Omprakash Pal was arrested for allegedly abducting and raping a minor girl. The FIR included charges under IPC Sections 363, 366, and 376. However, during the investigation, the prosecutrix and her mother gave statements not supporting the prosecution case.
Legal issues: Whether bail can be granted when key prosecution witnesses, including the victim, have not supported the prosecution's version of events.
Reasoning: The High Court considered the lack of support from the prosecutrix and her mother, the time already spent in custody, and the likelihood of delayed trial to grant bail, without commenting on the merits of the case.

text:
Pradeep Kumar Nehra vs Union Of India & Ors. (Delhi High Court, 2024-12-23). Outcome: Granted.
Outcome detail: Preventive detention order quashed; no bail granted but detention order under COFEPOSA invalidated
Summary: Delhi High Court quashed the preventive detention of Pradeep Kumar Nehra under COFEPOSA. The court ruled the detention unjustified since he was already in custody with no imminent release.
Facts: Pradeep Kumar Nehra was detained under the COFEPOSA Act for allegedly smuggling 2.4 kg of gold from Sharjah to Jaipur by concealing it in his sandals. He admitted to previous smuggling instances and connections with others in Dubai and Hyderabad. His electronic devices revealed detailed chats, voice notes, and transactions linked to a gold smuggling network.
Legal issues: Whether preventive detention under COFEPOSA is valid when the accused is already in custody with successive bail applications denied.
Reasoning: The court held that the detention order lacked application of mind as there was no material showing imminent possibility of the petitioner’s release from custody. Multiple bail rejections indicated no likelihood of immediate release, undermining justification for preventive detention.

Outcome detail: Bail cancelled by High Court after Sessions Court erroneously granted it despite earlier High Court rejection
Summary: High Court cancelled the bail granted to an accused involved in an education scam. The bail was improperly granted by a Magistrate despite earlier rejection by the High Court.
Facts: The accused, running an institution named Interactive Education, allegedly issued fake degrees, diplomas, and certificates without proper authorization, duping numerous students. The certificates spanned various courses and durations. After initially providing an undertaking to refund the money, the accused failed to comply. Despite the High Court denying bail, a Magistrate erroneously granted it.
Legal issues: Whether the Magistrate could grant bail contrary to a High Court order; whether issuance of unauthorized educational certificates amounts to fraud.
Reasoning: The High Court held that the Magistrate had committed judicial impropriety by granting bail after the High Court had already rejected the application. The accused had engaged in large-scale fraud by issuing fake educational credentials. His non-compliance with court orders and the seriousness of the offense necessitated bail cancellation.

text:
Radhika (Juvenile) vs State Of U.P. (Allahabad High Court, 2019-08-05). Outcome: Rejected.
Outcome detail: Bail application rejected by Special Judge POCSO Court; High Court directed application under Section 12 to be filed before Juvenile Justice Board
Summary: High Court rejected appeals of multiple juveniles including Radhika, ruling that bail must be sought through the Juvenile Justice Board under Section 12. It held juveniles over 16 involved in heinous offences are not entitled to bail as a matter of right.
Facts: Radhika, a juvenile, was accused in a case involving the death of her sister-in-law Jyoti due to alleged dowry-related bride burning. The deceased was married six months prior and reportedly suffered 95% burn injuries, with a dying declaration implicating Radhika. Juvenile Justice Board assessed her age and mental maturity, and transferred the case for adult trial.
Legal issues: Whether juveniles aged 16–18 can be denied bail and tried as adults under Section 15 and 18(3) of the Juvenile Justice Act; appropriate forum and legal standard for bail under such circumstances.
Reasoning: The court held that juveniles above 16 and involved in heinous offences cannot claim bail under Section 12 as a matter of right. It emphasized the need for a mental and physical assessment and directed that bail must be sought before the Juvenile Justice Board under Section 12. The appeal under Section 101(5) was found to be not maintainable.
Principles: Juveniles aged 16–18 involved in heinous crimes may be tried as adults under Section 18(3) of JJ Act; Bail under Section 12 is not a matter of right for such juveniles; Appeals under Section 101(5) not maintainable for bail denial by POCSO Courts; proper route is through the Board
